chunk_findings.detail: `_commits` runs `git log --no-renames --name-only --format=%x01%H%x1f%s <range>` and stores the parsed file list in `Commit.paths`. For merge commits git prints **no** paths with `--name-only` unless `-m`/`-c`/`--cc` is passed, so every merge commit in `HEAD..base` is recorded with `paths == ()`. Given the stated fixture "a gitflow repo where main is far ahead of develop (not behind)", the range is dominated by merge commits from landed PRs; each one is guaranteed to fail `_touches` and therefore lands in `DriftReport.unrelated` while `relevant` never contains it. A caller asking the DX-drift-notice question ("RELEVANT vs unrelated commits: touching globs, pin files, files the diff changed") gets a merge commit whose only content *was* the item's glob files reported as unrelated to them. Conflict-resolution ("evil merge") content is additionally invisible to `relevant` entirely.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/drift.py:_commits (and _touches/_touches-driven `relevant`)

chunk_findings.detail: `-m` (= `--diff-merges=separate`) makes git emit a **full diff for every parent** of a merge, and the new `seen` dict folds all of those per-parent path lists into a single `Commit.paths`. The diff against the *second* parent is not "what the merge brought" — it is the reverse: the mainline changes the merged branch had not yet seen. Concrete input: on `main`, commit `docs/d.md`; a `side` branch forked *before* that commit changes only `src/s.py`; then `git merge --no-ff side`. `git log -m --name-only` for that merge lists `src/s.py` (vs parent 1) *and* `docs/d.md` (vs parent 2). With `globs=["docs/"]`, `_touches` matches the merge, so `measure(...).relevant` reports a merge commit that never changed `docs/` as RELEVANT — exactly the "relevant vs unrelated commit" distinction DX-drift-notice is built on, and it gets worse the longer a branch was in flight (the second-parent diff is then the whole mainline delta). The new test does not cover this: `side` is forked at `main`'s tip and `main` gains nothing before the merge, so the second-parent diff is empty and the assertion passes. A first-parent-only diff (e.g. `--diff-merges=first-parent` semantics) is what "paths the merge brought" means; `-m` over-reports and makes unrelated merges match any glob that only the mainline touched.

chunk_findings.detail: The "added" branch guards the timestamp with `if d.at and ...`, but the "superseded" branch dereferences `d.at` unguarded. Given a state where decision `D` (`globs=["src/**"]`, no/None `at`) has `superseded_by="X"` and `X` has `at="2026-10-18T00:00:00Z"`, calling `decisions_changed(state, ["src/a.py"], "2026-10-01T00:00:00Z")` evaluates `None <= "2026-10-01T00:00:00Z"` and raises `TypeError: '<=' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'str'`, so the freshness/staleness check errors out instead of returning changes. If the missing timestamp is represented as `""` rather than `None`, the same line silently treats the decision as "recorded before `since_at`" and reports it as superseded even though its age is unknown — the exact case the `d.at` truthiness guard on the previous line was written to skip.

chunk_findings.detail: The `since` range drops the `HEAD` exclusion, so when `since` is an ancestor of `HEAD` (the normal case: last-seen base sha older than the tree's branch point) `since..base` is a strict superset of the actual drift `HEAD..base`. Example: base has B1..B5, the tree has already merged B1,B2, and `since=B1`; `behind` is computed as 3 (B3,B4,B5) but `_commits(tree, "B1..B5")` returns B2,B3,B4,B5, so `len(report.commits) == 4 != report.behind`, and if B2 touched one of the caller's globs it lands in `relevant` even though the tree already contains it — a "relevant commit" the operator has already merged, which is what the notice is meant to suppress. If `since` is not an ancestor of `base` at all (base branch rebased/force-pushed after the sha was stored, or the stored sha belongs to a different base branch), nothing is excluded and `since..base` degenerates to essentially the whole base history from the merge-base forward, so the same call floods `commits`/`relevant`/`unrelated` with the entire base history; no `merge-base --is-ancestor since base` check is made.

chunk_findings.detail: `moved_or_gone` returns `{}` when the `git diff` fails (`if not r.ok: return {}`), but `{}` is also the legitimate answer for "nothing moved". Callers cannot distinguish "could not tell" from "all paths are where they were", contradicting the module's own stated contract ("Could not tell is `behind=None`, never 0"). Concretely, a caller passes `since_sha=""` (e.g. `stamp()` returned `""` because the recorded base did not resolve), `git diff "" HEAD` fails, and PL-staleness (`paths missing/moved`) concludes every path is intact instead of reporting that the check could not run. The same fail-open happens for any invalid/unknown `since_sha`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/drift.py:moved_or_gone

chunk_findings.detail: The old `drift()` resolved an empty base itself — `base = base or drift_base(repo, here, cfg)` — so `drift(repo, here)` / `drift(repo, here, base="", cfg=cfg)` measured against the item's recorded `Item.base` or the repository default branch. The new body forwards the raw value straight through: `D.measure(repo, here, base, cfg=cfg, rulebooks=rulebooks())`. In the stated contract for the new core, `measure(repo, tree, base, ...)` takes `base` as a required argument and contains no fallback — the fallback logic lives in `base_of`, which is only reached via the `drift_base` shim that `drift` no longer calls. Given the documented default `base: str = ""` (kept on the signature and still advertised by the docstring "default: `drift_base`"), any caller that omits the base now reaches git with an empty rev range: `git rev-list --count HEAD..` is shorthand for `HEAD..HEAD`, which exits 0 with output `0`, so `measure` reports `behind == 0` and `drift` returns `Drift("", 0, ...)` — a silent "not behind / in sync" for a worktree that may be arbitrarily far behind its real base, instead of the base-resolved answer the old code produced. Either restore the `base or drift_base(repo, here, cfg)` resolution in `drift` (or guarantee it inside `measure` and drop the misleading `""` default).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce.py:2126 (drift)

chunk_findings.detail: The change adds exactly five baseline grants for the new module (moved_or_gone, decisions_changed, is_covered, last_seen, set_last_seen) and its own comment asserts the set is complete — "each helper's first caller is its consumer". But the module's described API also contains `stamp(repo, base) -> sha string for a created_at_sha field`. Nothing in this change wires a caller for it: `base_of` and `measure` are covered because `enforce.check_drift` imports and calls them, and the other five are listed precisely because their consumers (PL-staleness, DX-sync-command, DX-phase-suite-pass-sha, DX-drift-notice) do not exist yet. `stamp`'s only prospective consumer is DX-sync-points, which is not part of this change, so it lands as a new unreferenced function with no baseline grant. Concretely: run the unreferenced-functions guard over the tree built by this change; it reports `ddflow/services/drift.py:stamp` as unreferenced and not in the allowlist, so the guard fails on the very commit that introduces the module (and, if the guard also validates entries in both directions, the same omission is still the entry that must be added). Add `"ddflow/services/drift.py:stamp" = "DX-sync-points"` (or whatever task owns its first caller) alongside the other five lines.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/drift.py:stamp (tests/guard_baselines/unreferenced_functions.toml)

chunk_findings.detail: The new guard skips *every* governing decision whose own `at` is unset, before the supersession check, not just the timestamp comparison that used to raise. But a supersession is fully determinable without `D.at`: if `D.superseded_by` names `X` and `X.at > since_at`, then `X` (and therefore the `superseded_by` pointer on `D`, which can only have been written after `X` existed) is newer than the event, so `D` was superseded after `since_at` no matter what `D.at` is. Concretely, with `D` (`globs=["ddflow/services/**"]`, `at=None`, `superseded_by="X"`, `X.at="2026-10-18T00:00:00Z"`), `decisions_changed(state, ["ddflow/services/drift.py"], "2026-10-01T00:00:00Z")` returns `[]` instead of `[Change("D", "superseded")]`, so RR-freshness/PL-staleness report "no decision changed" although a decision governing the touched files was superseded after the recorded stamp — the exact class of silent staleness the function exists to prevent, and the inline comment ("neither added nor superseded can be told") is wrong for the superseded half. The probe named for the old finding only exercises a decision that *has* `at`, so it does not cover this input. The crash can be fixed without the loss by guarding only the comparison: keep `if d.at and d.at > since_at: out.append(Change(d.id, "added"))` and make the superseded branch `if by is not None and by.at and by.at > since_at and (d.at is None or d.at <= since_at):`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/drift.py:decisions_changed (`if not d.at: continue`)

chunk_findings.detail: The probe for the "`since` range drops the `HEAD` exclusion" finding cannot distinguish the fixed code from the buggy code, so it provides no evidence that the bug is fixed. In the test, `first = _commit(repo, "a.txt")` runs before the worktree is created, so `_tree(repo, "feat", "main", "T8")` branches `feat` from `main` at exactly `first`; nothing is ever committed on `feat`, so the tree's `HEAD` is `first` and `since == HEAD`. The buggy `rng = f"{since}..{base}"` therefore expands to `first..main`, which is the identical commit set as the correct `HEAD..main` (just `b.txt`); the buggy code also computes `behind` from `HEAD..main`, so it returns `behind == 1` and `len(commits) == 1` and the assertions pass unchanged. The divergence described in the finding only appears when the tree has *already integrated* commits that lie in `since..base`, e.g. `a = _commit("a.txt"); b = _commit("b.txt"); wt = _tree(...); c = _commit("c.txt"); D.measure(repo, wt, since=a)` — there the buggy range `a..main` returns `[b, c]` while `behind == 1`, and the pair `behind == 1 and len(commits) == 1` would fail. As written the test is satisfied by both the old and the new implementation, so prior finding #2 cannot be verified from this delta; the implementation half is needed or the test must be rewritten to commit into `main` between `first` and the worktree.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_drift_core.py:88 (`test_since_never_lists_what_the_tree_already_carries`)

In the stated contract for the new core, `measure(repo, tree, base, ...)` takes `base` as a required argument and contains no fallback — the fallback logic lives in `base_of`, which is only reached via the `drift_base` shim that `drift` no longer calls. Given the documented default `base: str = ""` (kept on the signature and still advertised by the docstring "default: `drift_base`"), any caller that omits the base now reaches git with an empty rev range: `git rev-list --count HEAD..` is shorthand for `HEAD..HEAD`, which exits 0 with output `0`, so `measure` reports `behind == 0` and `drift` returns `Drift("", 0, ...)` — a silent "not behind / in sync" for a worktree that may be arbitrarily far behind its real base, instead of the base-resolved answer the old code produced. Either restore the `base or drift_base(repo, here, cfg)` resolution in `drift` (or guarantee it inside `measure` and drop the misleading `""` default).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce.py:2126 (drift)

chunk_findings.detail: The change adds exactly five baseline grants for the new module (moved_or_gone, decisions_changed, is_covered, last_seen, set_last_seen) and its own comment asserts the set is complete — "each helper's first caller is its consumer". But the module's described API also contains `stamp(repo, base) -> sha string for a created_at_sha field`. Nothing in this change wires a caller for it: `base_of` and `measure` are covered because `enforce.check_drift` imports and calls them, and the other five are listed precisely because their consumers (PL-staleness, DX-sync-command, DX-phase-suite-pass-sha, DX-drift-notice) do not exist yet. `stamp`'s only prospective consumer is DX-sync-points, which is not part of this change, so it lands as a new unreferenced function with no baseline grant. Concretely: run the unreferenced-functions guard over the tree built by this change; it reports `ddflow/services/drift.py:stamp` as unreferenced and not in the allowlist, so the guard fails on the very commit that introduces the module (and, if the guard also validates entries in both directions, the same omission is still the entry that must be added). Add `"ddflow/services/drift.py:stamp" = "DX-sync-points"` (or whatever task owns its first caller) alongside the other five lines.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/drift.py:stamp (tests/guard_baselines/unreferenced_functions.toml)

chunk_findings.detail: The new guard skips *every* governing decision whose own `at` is unset, before the supersession check, not just the timestamp comparison that used to raise. But a supersession is fully determinable without `D.at`: if `D.superseded_by` names `X` and `X.at > since_at`, then `X` (and therefore the `superseded_by` pointer on `D`, which can only have been written after `X` existed) is newer than the event, so `D` was superseded after `since_at` no matter what `D.at` is. Concretely, with `D` (`globs=["ddflow/services/**"]`, `at=None`, `superseded_by="X"`, `X.at="2026-10-18T00:00:00Z"`), `decisions_changed(state, ["ddflow/services/drift.py"], "2026-10-01T00:00:00Z")` returns `[]` instead of `[Change("D", "superseded")]`, so RR-freshness/PL-staleness report "no decision changed" although a decision governing the touched files was superseded after the recorded stamp — the exact class of silent staleness the function exists to prevent, and the inline comment ("neither added nor superseded can be told") is wrong for the superseded half. The probe named for the old finding only exercises a decision that *has* `at`, so it does not cover this input. The crash can be fixed without the loss by guarding only the comparison: keep `if d.at and d.at > since_at: out.append(Change(d.id, "added"))` and make the superseded branch `if by is not None and by.at and by.at > since_at and (d.at is None or d.at <= since_at):`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/drift.py:decisions_changed (`if not d.at: continue`)

chunk_findings.detail: The probe for the "`since` range drops the `HEAD` exclusion" finding cannot distinguish the fixed code from the buggy code, so it provides no evidence that the bug is fixed. In the test, `first = _commit(repo, "a.txt")` runs before the worktree is created, so `_tree(repo, "feat", "main", "T8")` branches `feat` from `main` at exactly `first`; nothing is ever committed on `feat`, so the tree's `HEAD` is `first` and `since == HEAD`. The buggy `rng = f"{since}..{base}"` therefore expands to `first..main`, which is the identical commit set as the correct `HEAD..main` (just `b.txt`); the buggy code also computes `behind` from `HEAD..main`, so it returns `behind == 1` and `len(commits) == 1` and the assertions pass unchanged. The divergence described in the finding only appears when the tree has *already integrated* commits that lie in `since..base`, e.g. `a = _commit("a.txt"); b = _commit("b.txt"); wt = _tree(...); c = _commit("c.txt"); D.measure(repo, wt, since=a)` — there the buggy range `a..main` returns `[b, c]` while `behind == 1`, and the pair `behind == 1 and len(commits) == 1` would fail. As written the test is satisfied by both the old and the new implementation, so prior finding #2 cannot be verified from this delta; the implementation half is needed or the test must be rewritten to commit into `main` between `first` and the worktree.
